fixes.explanation: Annas it is, friend. He's Caiaphas's father-in-law, so the family tree is doing some work in this story. The text says they bring Jesus to him first, before anyone else. Caiaphas is the high priest that year (John 18:13).

Herod, the ruler of Galilee, is a name from another account of the trial (Luke 23:7), but John doesn't bring him in here. In this passage the soldiers take Jesus first to Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas, the high priest that year. Easy name to grab, though. Plenty of names are flying around this night.

Pilate, the Roman governor (Matthew 27:2), is a name from the trial accounts, but John 18:13 says they bring Jesus first to Annas. Annas is the father-in-law of Caiaphas, the high priest that year. Easy name to reach for, friend. This story has a lot of names in it.

This one's true, friend. The text says the other disciple goes into the courtyard of the high priest, and Peter stands outside at the door. He's not inside yet. Then the other disciple goes out, speaks to the doorkeeper and brings Peter in.

Silence would at least be quiet, but the text says Peter answers her. Her question is whether he's also one of this man's disciples, and he says, "I am not." That's a hard line to hear. I get a little quiet here too.

Nobody lights a fire to fix quiet, friend. A fire fixes cold, and cold is the reason the text gives. The servants and officers made a charcoal fire to keep warm. I've never once warmed my hands over a quiet room.
Teaching, yes. The high priest asks Jesus about His disciples and His teaching. Two things are on the table. Jesus answers next, so listen to that.
Miracles aren't on the list here. The text says the high priest questions Jesus about His disciples and His teaching. So the questions stay on who follows Him and what He taught.
Jesus doesn't send the high priest to the soldiers. He says, "Ask those who heard My message." The people to ask are the ones who heard Him. The soldiers aren't who He points to.

The teachers of the law don't come up in this exchange. Jesus tells the high priest, "Ask those who heard My message. Surely they know what I said." He points to those who heard Him. He says He taught in the synagogues and at the temple and said nothing in secret.

That's it. Jesus replies, "If I said something wrong, testify as to what was wrong. But if I spoke correctly, why did you strike Me?" It's a plain question. This is a heavy moment, and Jesus answers it straight.

Not this time, friend. When they ask him if he's one of Jesus' disciples, he denies it and says, "I am not." The text has Peter still standing and warming himself by the fire. This is a hard stretch, so I'll say it once: it's heavy.

Right away, a rooster crows. The text says Peter denied it once more, and immediately a rooster crowed. Earlier Jesus told Peter that the rooster wouldn't crow before Peter denied Him three times (John 13:38). That's the sound that follows.
The text never mentions the fire going out. What happens right after Peter denies it once more is that a rooster crows. It's one loud sound, and it matters.
